full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the pre-emptee who failed to resist pre-emption in both the courts below under section 96 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act (which shall hereinafter be called the Act). 

 (a) a transfer to a co-sharer in the tenancy whose interest has accrued otherwise than by purchase; or 

 Transfer in question was made on 31.1.80. Opposite party 1 had validly and legally transferred the property in question by way of gift by Ext. A to her husband opposite party 2 on 7.4.80 it was endorsed under section 60 on 17.9.80 that is, long before filing of the pre-emption case on 30.3.81. As such, it is apparent that on 30.3.81 when the case was filed the pre-emptee opposite party 1 had no title or any sa1cable or transferable interest in the case land. According to the recital of the deed, gift was made for love and affection of the son’s wife towards her father-in-law and for the good services rendered to him. For the aforesaid reasons it can be called that the transfer is an exchange not sale as has been illegally found by the courts below. So the transfer is not preemptible. A transfer by bequest or gift or by exchange, as I said, is excluded from the clutch of pre-emption both under sub-sections 10(b) and 10(c) of section 96 of the Act. Provision of section 96 (10)(b)(c) of the Act is no doubt ambiguous. Therefore, I accept the meaning of it which can be given by its interpretation or can be derived, to avoid injustice (Shamsuzzoha Nurul Amin vs, Province of East Pakistan, 22 DLR 377) court can modify the language of statute to effect the manifest and undoubted intention of the legislature. Md. Newjish Khan vs. Md. Amin 21 PLD 622 and Md. Amin Khan vs, Controller of State Duty, 13 DLR (SC) 105. It is well established rule of interpretation that a rule standard be interpreted in such a manner that it should he rather saved than destroyed. Dr. Neelima Ibrahim vs, People's Republic of Bangladesh, 32 DLR 201 and Dr. Nurul Islam vs. Bangladesh, 33 DLR (AD) 201 In view of the above position I find that the intention of the legislature was very clear to exclude transfers made by way of bequest (dictionary meaning will) and gift (Heba) affected in the form and nature as in the present case and also Heba-Bil-Ewaz when it is made without any pecuniary consideration. But a Heba-Bil-Ewaz when made in exchange of monetary consideration even within the three degrees of the donor of testator or beyond that the transfer is embraced within the scope of preemption under sub-section 10(c) of section 96 of the Act and it becomes pre-emptible. The reason is obvious and patent as because right of pre-emption is a right of prior purchase, in Bengali it is called অগ্রক্রয় and by pre-emption the pre-emptor purchases the property at the price at which it is transferred with statutory costs. In that view I hold that transfer by bequest (will or gift) Heba and Heba-Bil-Ewaz without any pecuniary consideration are excluded from pre-emption as the monetary value of those transactions cannot be calculated. 

 "love and affection cannot be measured in money and, as such, it cannot be said that the gift in question is a hiba-bil-ewaj wholly for consideration though partly the gift of exchange is for Rs 2000.00. In the aforesaid circumstances the gift in question is not a hiba-bil-ewaz as contemplated by section 96 of Bengal Tenancy Act and, as such, it cannot be pre-empted. Principles both in Bengal Tenancy Act and State Acquisition Act regarding pre-emption are same"
